hook: The king of Babylon who carved his laws in stone for everyone to read.

pages.x: Hammurabi became king of Babylon around 1792 BC, when it was one city among many stronger rivals. For thirty years he dug canals, built temples and walls, and made and broke alliances with neighbouring kings, waiting for his moment.

In a burst of wars late in his reign he beat Larsa in the south, Eshnunna in the east and even Mari, his old ally in the west, whose palace he burned. Babylon, once a minor town, was now the capital of all Mesopotamia and would stay its great city for over a thousand years.

He had 282 laws carved on a black stone pillar taller than a man, under a picture of himself receiving them from Shamash, the god of justice. They cover trade, wages, marriage, theft and doctors' fees. The most famous: if a man puts out another's eye, his own eye shall be put out. Punishments were harsher for the poor and slaves.

More than 150 of his letters survive on clay tablets. In them he orders canals cleared, settles quarrels over fields and debts, has a corrupt official brought to Babylon, and even tells a governor that the year needs an extra month added to the calendar.

About 600 years after Hammurabi, a king of Elam raided Babylon and carried the law stone home to Susa as a trophy. French archaeologists dug it up there in 1901, broken into three pieces. Today it stands in the Louvre in Paris.

Hammurabi was not the first king to write laws, but his are the best preserved and most famous. The idea that laws should be written down, public and applied case by case still shapes justice; his portrait is among the lawgivers carved in the US House of Representatives.
pts: Made Babylon the capital of Mesopotamia
Carved 282 laws in stone for all to see
Gave the world 'an eye for an eye'
